items.t: US soldier arrested in England on suspicion of espionage for Russia, police say
items.s: British police have arrested a 41-year-old member of the US military near Gloucester in southwest England on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia. The man is in custody, and the inquiry is continuing.
p: UK authorities say a man aged 41 who serves in the American armed forces was detained on Tuesday close to Gloucester, in the southwest of England. The Metropolitan Police in London suspects him of carrying out espionage on behalf of Russia. In a statement, the force said he was held under two parts of the National Security Act 2023, one dealing with help given to a foreign intelligence service and the other with obtaining or passing on protected information.

According to the force, its counter-terror officers worked hand in hand with the FBI and American military investigators. Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, who coordinates counterterrorism policing at national level, called the arrest significant and said the allegations are serious. She added that the inquiry is still moving forward. Police said officers were searching two addresses in Gloucestershire, and that the suspect is being held at a police station in the capital.

FBI Director Kash Patel described the arrest as important and said that espionage allegations of this kind worry Washington and its partners greatly. He warned that anyone who betrays their oath to the United States will face no tolerance. Sean Stinchon, who commands the US Army Counterintelligence Command, said the case showed how well the two countries’ agencies cooperate.

Police stressed that the detention has no link to other counter-terror inquiries. That suggests it is separate from a suspected Iran-linked plot in September at RAF Fairford, a British air base used by American forces. After that threat, the US Air Force pulled bombers from the site that had been deployed to hit Iran during the regional conflict.

A French broadcaster reported that the Americans also removed refuelling aircraft from the Royal Air Force base at Mildenhall in eastern England on Monday. It attributed the move, citing the Wall Street Journal, to a threat from Iran. That explanation reaches readers second-hand, through a newspaper account the broadcaster relayed.

DW noted that the Gloucestershire area contains several sensitive military and intelligence sites, and that nearby Cheltenham hosts the headquarters of GCHQ, Britain’s signals intelligence agency. These details describe the region rather than the case, and none of the reports connected them to the suspect.

The accounts also differ on his rank and role. One outlet called him a senior member of the US Army, while another described him only as a member of the US military. No source has named him, and none has reported charges or a court appearance.
items.cav: The suspect has not been named and no charges have been reported. Outlets differ on his seniority, and the Mildenhall link rests on a Wall Street Journal account relayed second-hand. The sources do not say what information was allegedly involved.
items.op: Espionage allegations against a serving soldier test both alliance cooperation and public trust. The man is presumed innocent, and authorities should bring charges or release details promptly and explain how the alleged breach happened. Secrecy around the case does little to protect national security.

items.t: Republicans pick Jim Jordan as House minority leader after midterm losses
items.s: House Republicans have chosen Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan, a close Trump ally, to lead their conference in the minority after losing the chamber in midterm elections. He succeeds Mike Johnson in the post.
p: Republicans in the US House of Representatives have elected Congressman Jim Jordan as their new minority leader, one week after losing their majority in the midterm elections. According to Al Jazeera, the vote was held by secret ballot on Tuesday, and Jordan won the support of his fellow party members over Majority Leader Steve Scalise.

The Guardian reported that Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January, with their largest margins in years. Sources describe the midterm defeat as sweeping, with Al Jazeera saying Democrats flipped at least 40 seats nationwide.

The role carries significant responsibilities. Jordan will shape the party’s response to the investigations Democrats have promised into Trump’s second term, and will help prepare for the 2028 presidential race. In a letter to colleagues before the vote, he described himself as “battle-tested” and called for a leadership team that is active and engaged.

Jordan is a longtime leader of the right in the House. He helped found the conservative Freedom Caucus, and as chairman of the House Oversight Committee he has investigated what he calls the weaponisation of government against Trump, including probes of former Special Counsel Jack Smith and Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis. Both have unsuccessfully prosecuted the president, according to Al Jazeera.

Supporters praised him as a fighter. Republican Congressman Brandon Gill wrote on social media that Jordan was “exactly what our Conference needs”. Some Republicans, including Tennessee lawmaker Tim Burchett, said the party needed to admit mistakes after the defeat.

Jordan has faced past allegations, which he denies, that he knew of sexual abuse of student-athletes by a physician at Ohio State University, where he once worked as an assistant wrestling coach. Al Jazeera reported those allegations without establishing any finding against him.

Democrats criticised the choice. Virginia congressman Don Beyer said Republicans had “learned absolutely nothing” from the election, and linked the decision to Trump’s recent appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff.
items.cav: The sources differ in emphasis: Al Jazeera frames the vote around unity and the opposition agenda, while The Guardian centres on the party’s change of strategy and Democratic criticism. Former House Speaker Mike Johnson’s plans were reported only by The Guardian, and the outcome of the allegations against Jordan is not described in the evidence.
items.op: Parties are entitled to choose their own leaders, but a minority that has lost voters’ confidence owes the public a clear account of what went wrong. Jordan’s record of confrontation with prosecutors and investigators makes it fair to ask whether he will offer scrutiny of the majority, or simply more fighting. Voters should judge that by his conduct in opposition.

items.t: Hegseth Rebuffs Impeachment Push With Rare Pentagon Press Conference
items.s: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held a rare news conference at the Pentagon to dismiss an impeachment effort led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie. His remarks focused more on defending President Trump than on answering the charges.
p: Hegseth met reporters at the Pentagon at 8am on a Tuesday, according to the Guardian, after avoiding press briefings for nearly six months. The session came as an unpopular war with Iran continued during an election campaign.

The trigger was Massie, the outgoing Republican congressman from Kentucky, who has introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. The Guardian reports that the articles are likely to win support from Democrats and possibly some Republicans.

The charges, as described in the report, include waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and violating the War Powers Resolution, which requires US forces to withdraw from unauthorized hostilities after 60 days. Other accusations cover strikes against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean, the capture of Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, strikes against Yemen, and retaliation against Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat who urged military members to disobey illegal orders. Hegseth is named in these accusations but has not been found guilty of anything; they remain allegations.

Hegseth described the effort as a “farce” and said no secretary of war or defense had been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations. He compared the case with past conflicts under Republican and Democratic presidents, arguing that none had led to impeachment.

He did not name Massie during the 25-minute appearance, instead calling him “disgruntled” several times. Hegseth said the effort reflected “policy disagreements” rather than the offenses the founders had in mind when they wrote the impeachment clause.

Hegseth also invoked his predecessor, Lloyd Austin, saying Austin had not faced impeachment after a troubled withdrawal from Afghanistan and a period of medical treatment for cancer. He said the matter was not about him, and warned that if critics wanted to pursue the military, they would have to go through him.

The defense secretary framed the impeachment effort as an attack on President Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term. Hegseth said he was proud to stand with the president, and accused the media of being unable to acknowledge Trump’s military success against Iran because they “hate the president”. The Guardian’s account does not include independent verification of claims about the war’s outcome.
The Guardian’s commentary suggests the press conference was aimed as much at the White House as at reporters in the room.
items.cav: The impeachment articles are allegations, and the evidence does not say whether the House will vote on them. The report is a commentary piece with a critical tone, and its characterisations, such as the description of Hegseth’s remarks, are the outlet’s own reading. Hegseth’s claims about the Iran war are not independently confirmed in the source.
items.op: Impeachment is a constitutional tool, and serious accusations about war powers and civilian harm deserve a factual answer. Calling the process a farce and attacking critics as disgruntled does not explain the legal basis for the conduct under review. Transparency means answering questions under oath and in the open, not in a single appearance that avoids the charges.

items.t: Najib Razak leaves prison for house arrest at his Kuala Lumpur home
items.s: Former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak is now at home, where he will finish his corruption sentence under house arrest. The move follows a royal pardon and a High Court ruling that took effect straight away.
p: Najib, 73, reached his Kuala Lumpur residence late on Tuesday night, according to the BBC. Reporters and photographers gathered outside as he arrived by SUV, with police vehicles accompanying him. The home, located in an upscale part of the capital, has been designated a federal prison.

His return closes a four-year period behind bars. He was found guilty of taking billions of dollars from the national investment fund 1MDB, a case that toppled his administration and reached figures in Malaysia, at Goldman Sachs and in Hollywood. Investigators put the amount drained from the fund at $4.5bn, with part of it flowing into private hands, including his own. Prosecutors allege that more than $1bn landed in accounts connected to him.

In September, the monarch approved a conditional pardon that lets Najib serve his last two years at home. A planned move on Friday was delayed when the attorney general asked for clarity on the royal decree. On Tuesday, the High Court determined that the house arrest could begin right away. As part of the pardon conditions, his party handed over a $12m fine.

A 2020 verdict in the first trial gave him 12 years for abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust. The case concerned 42 million ringgit moved from SRC International, a former 1MDB subsidiary. He entered prison in 2022, and an appeal later cut the term by half.

A second trial, concluded in December 2025, produced a 15-year sentence linked to nearly 2.3 billion ringgit taken from 1MDB. He is challenging that ruling, and he is set to begin that term once house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

Najib, who led the government from 2009 to 2018, has rejected any wrongdoing. His legal team argues that advisers misled him, especially the financier Jho Low, who insists on his own innocence and is still at large.
Critics argue that his release weakens anti-corruption work and question whether it has a legal foundation, since they say Malaysian law does not provide for house arrest.
items.cav: The sources do not explain the High Court's reasoning, and critics' view that the legal basis is weak remains contested rather than settled. The $4.5bn and $1bn figures are investigators' and prosecutors' estimates and allegations, not established totals. Najib's appeal against the second sentence is pending.
items.op: A convicted leader moving from cell to mansion on a legal basis critics dispute tests whether anti-corruption rules bind the powerful. Malaysia should publish the royal decree and the court's full reasoning. Without that, the 1MDB verdicts risk looking negotiable.

items.t: First day of Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi called constructive, with key disputes unresolved
items.s: Officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States held the first of two days of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. Kyiv and Washington described the session as positive, but the central disagreement over eastern Ukraine remains.
p: Senior officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States met in Abu Dhabi for the first trilateral talks since February, with a second day scheduled for Wednesday. Delegations from Kyiv, Washington and Moscow took part in four hours of discussions, according to the BBC.

Russian and Ukrainian officials said little publicly after the session. President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved “constructive and quite substantive”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking from Paris, called the meeting “very productive”. Zelensky said humanitarian issues, including prisoner of war exchanges, had also been discussed.

Expectations for a breakthrough were low. US officials said Moscow and Kyiv were showing “a little bit of flexibility” in private on who would control Ukraine’s eastern regions after a war ends. Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, told delegates the two sides had “narrowed the gaps”, but gave no details.

The core dispute concerns Donetsk, which Russia largely occupies. Moscow wants Ukraine to give up the parts it still holds, while Kyiv wants the current contact line frozen so it keeps control of those areas, which it says are vital to its security. A US official said the territorial question cannot be settled before the shape of a post-war “security architecture” is agreed.

The framework under discussion reportedly includes security consultations, crisis communication hotlines and “reciprocal de-escalation measures”. Officials also floated reviving the Nato-Russia Council, which has been largely paused since 2022. European leaders, long excluded from the talks, have pushed to take part, and Rubio said Europeans “are a part of solving this problem”. A US official, however, said the Russians have “a bad taste in their mouth” about Europe.

Scepticism is widespread. The previous round in Geneva in February ended without a breakthrough, and talks stalled after the US-Israel war on Iran drew Washington’s attention away. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, who heads the parliamentary foreign affairs committee, told the BBC he believed Trump wanted “a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine”, and argued that more sanctions and deep strikes were needed to push Moscow into real negotiations.
items.cav: Zelensky did not attend, and the claims of private flexibility come from an unnamed US official, so they cannot be independently checked. Kushner’s claim that the gaps had narrowed was given without details, and the outcome of the second day was not yet known when the reporting was published.
items.op: Peace terms that decide the fate of eastern Ukraine and its security should not be shaped in closed rooms and described through anonymous briefings. Ukraine and its European neighbours have a direct stake and deserve a seat, with the substance made public. Transparency is the real test of whether this round means progress.

items.t: Israel’s new parliament sworn in as Eisenkot tries to form a government without a majority
items.s: Israel’s new Knesset has been sworn in, but neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot holds a majority. Eisenkot has been given the first chance to build a government.
p: Israel’s parliament has taken its oath, but the vote count leaves the country without a clear route to a new government. Neither the bloc behind caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor the opposition camp led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot controls the 120-seat Knesset.

According to the BBC, Eisenkot’s alliance of four parties took 48 seats in October’s election, while Netanyahu’s bloc won 53. President Isaac Herzog has handed Eisenkot the task of forming a cabinet, because more Knesset members recommended him for the role than recommended Netanyahu. The BBC notes that some of those who backed Eisenkot are not prepared to sit in the same government.

Eisenkot has four weeks to assemble a coalition, and can ask for a further two weeks, according to the BBC. Netanyahu stays in office in a caretaker capacity while talks continue, and that period could last anywhere from a few days to several months.

Both leaders used the swearing-in to attack each other. Netanyahu asked lawmakers whether they were willing to rely on parties that want to destroy the Jewish state, a reference to any Eisenkot government that would depend on Arab parties. He also urged a unity government to face what he called the threat of “a nuclear Iran”. Eisenkot, for his part, proposed a “national emergency government” that would set ideological disputes aside in order to remove Netanyahu.

The two Arab-led lists, the United Arab List and the Joint List, took 19 seats between them, a record gained after Arab voter turnout rose sharply. That gives them potential leverage over the outcome. Netanyahu has ruled out working with them, and several parties in Eisenkot’s bloc oppose including them. The United Arab List, with eight seats, has said it is ready to join an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, with 11, has offered to back such a government from outside.

Eisenkot has set four conditions for any party or lawmaker who wants to join him: recognising Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence, backing compulsory service for everyone including groups now exempt, and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must lose its military and governing capacity. The BBC reports that these conditions could prove difficult for some potential partners. The ultra-Orthodox parties, with 13 seats between them, have strongly opposed any change to the exemption from military service, which was a central issue in the campaign.

Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a government that depends on Arab lawmakers. Another report says he has proposed an alliance with the ultra-Orthodox parties instead. The opposition also plans to use its new legislative weight to press for an inquiry into security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.
items.cav: The sources do not say which parties would ultimately back Eisenkot, and the price the ultra-Orthodox parties would demand is described only as likely to involve major concessions on conscription. Arab parties’ willingness to help rests on their public statements, not on agreed deals.
items.op: Coalition talks in Israel should be judged by how openly their terms are put to voters. Eisenkot’s four conditions give the public a clear test of commitment to democracy and the rule of law. Any party that rejects them should explain its reasons in public, and any deal struck behind closed doors should be disclosed to the electorate before it takes office.

items.t: Inside Slovyansk, a shrinking front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
items.s: The BBC gained access to a Ukrainian drone unit defending Slovyansk, one of four fortress cities in eastern Donetsk, where residents say constant bombardment is forcing people to leave.
p: Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in parts of Donetsk still under Ukrainian control. According to the BBC, Russia wants Kyiv to give up these cities, and they are central to peace talks that resumed in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the US after a nine-month pause.

The BBC’s reporters were escorted into the city by members of a drone unit that calls itself Peaky Blinders. Tetiana, 21, and her colleague Yasha scan their phones for military intelligence on likely threats from the air. Military escorts described the rainy, overcast weather as good, because drones struggle in such conditions.

The city is under constant attack from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs. Abandoned vehicles line the streets, according to the report, having been destroyed by remotely operated first-person-view drones. Anti-drone netting covers the roads, but the BBC said it offers no guarantee of safety. Tetiana said walking was safer than driving.

Very little of the city has been left unscathed. The BBC saw a school destroyed by glide bombs, a gaping hole in a residential block, and boarded-up shops, most of them closed. Tetiana said Russia is trying to intimidate residents into fleeing “in chaos”, a strategy she described in stark terms.

Before the war, Slovyansk had more than 200,000 residents, and the BBC reports that fewer than 10% remain. Iryna, who works in one of the city’s last cafes, said she had already lost her home but would not leave: “I won’t leave Slovyansk. This is my home.” Inga, 53, said she stays because she has nowhere else to go and no money to start again.

The report cites Ukraine’s general staff as saying more than 54,000 Russian troops were killed or injured in October, the deadliest month for Russian forces since the full-scale invasion began. Russia has taken nearly 90% of the Donbas, but its advances this year have largely stalled. Commander Oleksandr of the drone unit told the BBC that neither side can advance because of the number of drones in use.

The White House has sounded positive about the revived talks, despite President Volodymyr Zelensky’s refusal to cede territory. Ukrainians fear that handing over the fortress cities would make it easier for Russia to push further west, including towards Kyiv.
items.cav: The 54,000 casualty figure comes from Ukraine’s general staff and is not independently verified in the report, and no Russian response is included. The drone unit’s link to the Omega National Guard Special Forces, mentioned in the report, is not explained.
items.op: Civilians in Slovyansk should not be treated as bargaining chips in any settlement. Any deal that trades away cities should be open to public scrutiny, with clear guarantees for the people who still live there.

items.t: Italian coalition split over Ukraine aid as minister's signature on thirteenth package is pending
items.s: Italy's governing coalition is divided over a thirteenth military and civilian aid package for Ukraine, which cannot be published until League Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti signs it. The dispute comes as Rome has won a seat at peace talks in Abu Dhabi, according to Euronews.
p: On Tuesday 10 November, Defence Minister Guido Crosetto was due to present the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine to Copasir, the Parliamentary Committee for the Security of the Republic. Giorgetti, however, has not yet signed the measure, which the procedure requires.

Within the governing majority, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Crosetto have played down the episode. They pointed to Crosetto's absence, since he had been in Brussels for the Ecofin meeting on Monday. Tajani also said the document is classified and must be signed in person, not electronically.

Crosetto, speaking to the daily Repubblica, said he was convinced Giorgetti would sign once he returned from Brussels. He also defended continued support for Kyiv and stressed the need for a common European position, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has requested. Sources at Palazzo Chigi repeated that Europe must speak with one voice, even as talks began in Abu Dhabi.

The row is rooted in the League's stance. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini has repeatedly voiced reservations about military aid to Kyiv, while Meloni, together with Forza Italia, has remained firm on supporting Ukraine for as long as necessary. Salvini's position has hardened since a League congress reconfirmed him as party secretary.

League senator Claudio Borghi has increased the pressure on social media, describing the package as a “decree that does not exist” because a measure requiring joint ministerial approval does not exist until all the ministers have signed it.

Without Giorgetti's signature the decree cannot be published, and neither the military nor the civilian aid can be sent. Reporting by Euronews warns that this could open a serious fight inside the majority whose consequences are hard to predict.

According to the report, the package is expected to include civilian aid such as generators and probably air-defence weapons. Because a Franco-Italian Samp-T battery was supplied earlier, the shipment could include Aster missiles for that system. The details remain classified, as all previous packages have been.

Many in the majority reportedly believe Giorgetti will sign in the end, since a breakdown could threaten the centre-right government while it is working through the budget. The mechanism rests on a framework decree introduced by the Draghi government in 2022, which has been renewed four times and expires at the end of the year. Under it, twelve packages have been approved in four years, requiring only a briefing to the Copasir committee.

The most recent package was sent at the end of 2025. A new framework decree, adopted shortly after Christmas, authorises military and civilian supplies to Ukraine for the whole of 2026. The report does not say how the current impasse will be resolved.
items.cav: The account relies on one outlet and on unnamed government sources, and Crosetto's confidence that Giorgetti will sign is his own claim. Because the package is classified, the list of contents is described as probable rather than confirmed.
items.op: A military aid decision should not hang on one minister's private timing inside a coalition feud. Parliament and the public deserve a clear account of who must sign, when, and why. Classified does not mean unaccountable, and the framework's joint-approval design only works if every signature is given in good faith.

items.t: France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge cyberattack, Tehran denies role
items.s: France has summoned Iran’s ambassador and says it will seek European Union sanctions over a cyberattack that disrupted hundreds of supermarkets. Tehran rejects the accusations as baseless.
p: Paris has summoned Iran’s ambassador after accusing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration. Iran’s Foreign Ministry rejected the accusations on Tuesday, calling them baseless and one-sided and condemning what it described as a habitual practice of blaming the Islamic Republic.

The alleged attack began overnight on October 11 and 12. According to French prosecutors, it targeted roughly 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets by remotely starting abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles and disabling temperature alerts. Retailers said perishable food was thrown away, with millions of euros’ worth spoiled. In some cases, the heat caused fires or melted equipment. Several large French chains, including E-Leclerc, Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U, were affected.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said she had opened an investigation into members of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit she described as an offensive unit linked to the IRGC’s electronic and cyber centre. Her office has requested arrest warrants for two of its officials and is looking into others. French cyber intelligence agencies said the unit primarily targeted Israel and the United States, but also France and other European countries.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the government would rule nothing out in response and would push for EU sanctions. He said the aim was to deter anyone tempted to repeat the attack. Tehran responded by warning it would take measures to protect its interests and accused France of covering up its own governance failures. Relations between the two countries were already strained after expulsions of diplomats in August.

Other incidents are harder to pin down. A suspected attack on November 2 caused temperature spikes in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden, and a failed attempt on cooling units at French blood banks was reported this month. Officials have not said whether these events are connected. Sweden’s civil defence minister warned that more attacks could follow in the coming months.

Cybersecurity expert Jody Westby told Al Jazeera that tracing the group responsible is very difficult because of weak international cooperation on cybercrime. The evidence published so far consists largely of French official statements, while Iran has offered only a denial.
items.cav: The attribution to the IRGC comes from French officials and has not been independently verified in the sources. Whether the later incidents in Sweden, Belgium and elsewhere are linked remains unclear, and the sources give no details of the evidence behind the arrest warrant requests.
items.op: Serious accusations of state-linked sabotage need public evidence before sanctions follow. Paris should publish what it can, so that citizens and allies can judge the case rather than simply trust the government’s word.

items.t: US Inflation Runs Hotter Than Forecast in October as Tariffs and Oil Weigh on Prices
items.s: Consumer prices in the United States rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% analysts had expected, adding to pressure on the Federal Reserve ahead of its December meeting. The official figures came a week after the midterm elections.
p: Official figures show US prices rose 0.4% over October, slower than the 0.6% increase recorded in September but above what economists had forecast. Analysts said the result strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates when it meets in December.
The increase was driven mainly by higher housing, food and energy costs. Energy prices rose 0.7% in October, a much smaller gain than the 5.2% jump in September, according to the figures as reported.

No annual inflation rate was published this month. The Bureau of Labor Statistics normally reports a 12-month change, but it did not collect data in October 2025, so it cannot calculate that comparison.

The Bureau measures inflation through the consumer price index, which tracks the prices of hundreds of everyday goods and services, from groceries and petrol to medical care. Its basket of goods is updated over time as spending habits change.

The sources link the energy trend to the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran. Crude oil was trading at just over $70 a barrel before the war began, but it has since risen above $100, reportedly because supplies were constricted.

Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller, who spoke before the October figures were released, reportedly signalled he was leaning towards a rate rise in December even if inflation came in slower than expected.

Tariffs are also part of the picture. After the Supreme Court struck down most of the additional global tariffs in February, the president announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. According to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, American businesses absorbed nearly 90% of the cost of the new levies, because overseas exporters cut their prices only slightly.

The New York Fed also found that each one-percentage-point rise in average tariffs pushed up consumer goods prices by nearly 0.25% after a year. Inflation is still well below the peaks seen during the Covid pandemic, when supply chain disruptions pushed prices sharply higher.
items.cav: The sources describe October's rise as both faster-than-expected and as 0.4% against a forecast of 0.3%, and they do not give a full 12-month figure. The oil price and Waller’s stance are reported second-hand, and the tariff cost estimates come from a New York Fed study that the sources summarise rather than publish in full.
items.op: Official data gaps and trade policy are now shaping household budgets and central bank decisions. Policymakers owe the public clear explanations of how tariffs feed into prices, and the Bureau should restore complete data collection without delay. Voters deserve numbers they can check.

items.t: US, Russia and Ukraine open Abu Dhabi talks as strikes on Ukrainian energy continue
items.s: Delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States began US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, the first substantive round in months, as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued. US officials described the first day as productive.
p: The talks in the United Arab Emirates are the first substantive negotiations in months and focus on ending a conflict that has lasted more than four years. The first day ended after about four hours, and the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service said the sessions were expected to resume the next morning. Ukrainian negotiators also met representatives from NATO and Europe as part of their mission.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks “very productive” but said a lot of work remained. According to Reuters, he also said the aim was, at some point, to widen the trilateral format to include other European voices. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff said there were “some good ideas” for bridging the gap between what Moscow and Kyiv want from a peace deal.

The talks followed a night of attacks. Ukraine’s prime minister, Sergii Koretskyi, said Russia had hit five major energy substations in the Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad regions. The state grid operator Ukrenergo reported outages in several other regions. Citing the Kyiv Independent, The Guardian reported that Russian attacks had killed at least nine people across Ukraine over the previous day. Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of stepping up strikes to pressure Kyiv before the talks.

Europe’s role remains contested. A joint statement from US, European and Ukrainian negotiators spoke of a “shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture”, but it is unclear whether all sides mean the same thing. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said any discussion of Europe’s security architecture should wait until a ceasefire is in place and take place in a forum that includes NATO allies and EU members.

The composition of the delegations has drawn attention. Kyiv has kept largely the same team, led by Rustem Umerov, which signals continuity in its push for a ceasefire. Moscow is led by Vladimir Medinsky, but has also brought Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, who helped draft Russia’s December 2021 security demands to NATO. Euronews reported that his presence raises the possibility that Moscow wants to widen the agenda beyond Ukraine. The Institute for the Study of War has suggested that his experience could be used to undermine Ukraine’s push for security guarantees.

Donald Trump has said that an eventual agreement would be “a big agreement” and would involve more than Ukraine. Neither Washington nor Moscow has said whether NATO’s wider security arrangements are on the agenda. The reporting so far does not settle that question, and the public record on the scope of the talks is thin.
items.cav: Casualty and damage figures come from Ukrainian officials and secondhand reports, and they vary between outlets. The figure of at least nine dead was cited by The Guardian from the Kyiv Independent. The scope of any agreement on European security has not been confirmed by either Washington or Moscow.
items.op: Talks that could reshape Europe’s security order should not be settled without the countries most affected at the table. Washington and Moscow have not said whether NATO arrangements are on the agenda, and that silence is the problem. Any deal must be public and must have Ukraine’s and Europe’s consent.

items.t: Hegseth dismisses House impeachment push over Iran war as a “farce” that would fail
items.s: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has called a move by outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie to impeach him a farce that would fail. Hegseth told reporters on Tuesday that the effort targets policy disagreements, not impeachable offences.
p: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday dismissed a push to impeach him over his conduct of the war against Iran, calling it a farce that would not succeed. He spoke at his first press briefing from the Pentagon in six months, a session that came as the Trump administration faces criticism over the conflict.

The impeachment resolution was filed in the House on Monday by Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger and is leaving Congress. Massie says Hegseth’s actions amount to “high crimes and misdemeanors” and that his leadership “warrants impeachment”.

The resolution focuses mainly on the Iran war but also refers to Hegseth’s role in military actions in Yemen, against Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, and in Venezuela. Hegseth rejected the case, telling reporters that no defence secretary in the country’s 250-year history had been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations.

Hegseth described the move as a “political spectacle” by an opponent of President Donald Trump. In a video posted on social media last week, he said impeachment was about “the politics of personal destruction”. The Pentagon’s top spokesman, Sean Parnell, said Hegseth was fully committed to leading the department until the end of Trump’s term, and cast the effort as a “sham witch hunt” by Democrats.

A House vote could come by midweek, according to the reporting, which says the next steps are highly uncertain. The vote would put pressure on Republicans, many of whom have blamed their heavy losses in last week’s midterm elections at least partly on the Iran conflict and its economic impact.

Trump has backed Hegseth. He pointed to a January raid that captured then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, and to military operations against Iran that he says have “obliterated” Iran’s navy and air force. Trump told reporters on Monday that the Iran war was “militarily effectively over” and said Iran would like to make a deal.

The picture on the ground is less settled. Iran has continued to strike US military bases in the Middle East and has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global oil prices, during a conflict now more than eight months old. The US military has also kept up intermittent operations against Iran and fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.

Hegseth framed his defence in terms of litigation, saying that if critics want to examine the military actions, he is willing to do so. Whether the House will act on the resolution, and what it would mean for Hegseth’s position, remains unclear from the available reporting.
items.cav: The report relies on the statements of Hegseth, Massie, Trump and Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell, and the claims about the war’s status are contested by the reported Iranian strikes. The timing of a House vote and its outcome are not confirmed.
items.op: Impeachment is a constitutional remedy, not a verdict on political disagreement. Whatever the House decides, the Iran war’s legal basis and costs deserve open scrutiny, and officials should answer specific questions rather than dismiss them as a farce.

items.t: US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks open in Abu Dhabi amid disputes over security guarantees and territory
items.s: Talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, November 10, in what reports describe as the first substantive round since February. The two-day session is expected to focus on security guarantees for the warring countries.
p: Delegations opened the talks in the capital of the United Arab Emirates as Washington pressed again for a settlement. According to the Guardian, US officials say they want the conflict to be definitively concluded. The first day wrapped up early in the afternoon local time, and a second session was scheduled for Wednesday.

The Trump administration’s approach includes drawing up a new security framework between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said. European officials worry that Moscow will keep pressing for Nato to scale back its military presence across eastern Europe, a move they fear could leave allies exposed to Russian influence.

Before the trilateral session, European officials met separately with Ukrainian and American representatives and issued a joint statement. It said any future arrangements must uphold national borders, political independence and the right of each country to make its own decisions, and must offer dependable protection for Ukraine. Reports list the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Nato and the European Commission among those taking part in the separate discussions.

US officials said Washington had raised with Moscow security guarantees for Ukraine modelled on Nato’s Article 5, the collective defence clause. Critics doubt what would activate such guarantees, pointing out that the clause does not require members to defend one another and that cyberattacks and hybrid tactics have blurred the threshold for a military response. Euronews, citing US media, adds that the discussions also touched on Article 4, which provides for consultations.

On territory, US media reported, citing a senior American official, that both Ukraine and Russia had privately signalled some willingness to compromise over disputed land. The official gave no specifics. President Donald Trump has suggested Ukraine could emerge from the war with altered borders, without saying which changes he has in mind. Moscow insists that Kyiv recognise Russian control over Crimea and four Ukrainian regions, and Kyiv rejects those terms.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his team would put forward steps to reduce fighting in Abu Dhabi and would seek agreement on setting up a trilateral meeting of leaders. Ukraine’s chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, named ending hostilities, securing guarantees after the war, economic recovery and humanitarian measures as Kyiv’s priorities. Zelenskyy also accused Russia of striking bridges and the power grid in an effort to split Ukraine along the Dnipro River.

Washington has warned against expecting a quick breakthrough. Jared Kushner, a lead US negotiator, called the conflict highly complicated and said the talks could help move the process to its next stage. Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed some progress has been made on the shape of the future architecture, though the details of the proposals remain unclear.
items.cav: Sources differ on the security guarantees: the Guardian reports discussion of Article 5 only, while Euronews, citing US media, also mentions Article 4. The territorial “flexibility” comes from an unnamed official who gave no details, so it is second-hand and unverified. The evidence contains no direct response from Moscow to the US proposals.
items.op: Any settlement that trades territory or redraws Europe’s security map should be negotiated in the open, with Kyiv and European capitals genuinely at the table. Deals struck over the heads of the people most affected repeat the mistake behind Russia’s 2021 ultimatum. The test is whether any guarantees are written down, enforceable and subject to public scrutiny.

items.t: Hegseth calls Massie impeachment bid a ‘political spectacle’ as Iran war scrutiny grows
items.s: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed articles of impeachment brought against him by Republican congressman Thomas Massie, describing them as a stunt and a political spectacle. Speaking at his first news conference in six months, he defended the conduct of US military operations.
p: Hegseth took the podium at the Pentagon and immediately attacked the articles of impeachment that Massie, an outgoing Republican, introduced on Monday. He said the effort was not oversight or accountability, and described it as driven by ego and resentment. He also said it would harm the warriors who defend the country.

Hegseth said that the articles were baseless and that every operation cited in them was lawful. He listed Iran, the cartels, Maduro and Yemen, saying each was carried out under orders from the commander-in-chief, then from himself, and was notified to Congress. He claimed the strikes had destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities, sank boats carrying drugs and put a “narco dictator” in handcuffs. He insisted none of this amounted to high crimes.

According to the Guardian’s live coverage, the House has until Wednesday to act on the articles. Lawmakers can hold a floor vote, send the resolution to committee for further investigation, or table it entirely. Hegseth framed the dispute as a policy disagreement that should be settled through legislation and debate, while calling the effort an act of sabotage.

The press conference also touched on the wider political fallout of the war, which the Guardian said is now in its eighth month. After several Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, linked the party’s midterm losses to the conflict and rising prices, Hegseth declined to say whether he agreed. He pointed instead to Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s view that the war was “not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary”, and said he shared that view.

Hegseth told reporters that the media had ignored military successes and accused some of hating the president more than the country. He also noted that 150 years had passed since a defence secretary was last impeached. He was referring to William Belknap, who served under President Ulysses S Grant and was impeached in 1876. The Senate later acquitted him. Hegseth placed the current effort alongside the impeachments of Donald Trump in 2019 and 2021, saying they had failed.

Separately, flight-tracking data showed that the US had withdrawn at least a dozen aircraft, including refuelling tankers, from Mildenhall Royal Air Force base in eastern England on Monday. The Wall Street Journal reported that the move followed a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with events. According to the Journal, as relayed by AFP, the precise nature of that threat was still under discussion among US officials.

The US military said it was taking “coordinated and appropriate” security steps. A spokesperson for its European Command declined to discuss specific force protection measures, noting that various factors can affect them.
items.cav: The Guardian coverage is a live blog and may be updated, and Hegseth’s claims that every strike was lawful are his own assertions, not findings. The Mildenhall withdrawal is second-hand, based on flight-tracking data and unnamed people cited by the Wall Street Journal, and the Iranian threat itself remains unspecified. The BBC material available here is only a summary.
items.op: Whatever one thinks of the Iran war, a defence secretary’s legal justification for it should be tested, not dismissed as a stunt. Calling a congressional challenge sabotage does not answer the questions it raises. Impeachment exists so that claims of lawful conduct are examined in public, and Hegseth’s refusal to engage on the merits weakens that check.

items.t: Former NATO chief says Europe must earn its seat in Ukraine talks, not plead for one
items.s: Former NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen told Euronews that Europe must earn a role in the US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine by offering something useful. He warned that complacency could leave the continent in lasting conflict.
p: Rasmussen argued that Europe is currently in a weak bargaining position and should stop asking for a place among the negotiators. In his view, European governments need to bring capabilities that the talks cannot do without, and he said he hopes they will recognise the urgency now.

He spoke as Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, with the stated aim of ending Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Officials from the EU, NATO, Britain, Germany, Italy and France were also travelling to the United Arab Emirates, but for separate discussions and not the main three-way meeting.

Jared Kushner, an adviser to US President Donald Trump and his son-in-law, said last week that the talks would focus on a new European security order. Russian officials have used similar wording when calling for a smaller NATO presence in Europe. Rasmussen accused Washington of choosing Moscow and siding with Vladimir Putin.

Divisions among European leaders surfaced after the Norwegian prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, held a 90-minute call with Putin. Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen said she was doubtful of the move, which she said had not been coordinated with other leaders.

Rasmussen, a former Danish prime minister, said that speaking to Moscow was sensible in principle, but such initiatives should be planned together. He also rejected the idea that Europe could act as an impartial go-between, saying it would stand with Ukraine.

Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has insisted that eastern European states must have a voice in any settlement, since they face the spillover effects of the war most directly. Asked whether their security concerns should shape the negotiations, Rasmussen said eastern Europeans should have been heard earlier. He led NATO from 2009 to 2014, and Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had joined the alliance and the EU in 2004, just before his tenure.

Rasmussen also faulted Washington for holding up approval of US-made air-defence missiles for Ukraine. Zelenskyy said in late October that he had waited nearly a month for Patriot and NASAMS deliveries, and Rasmussen called the holdup a serious blow to Ukraine’s defences. Asked whether NATO had ever been this divided, given US troop cuts, Trump’s threats to leave the alliance and the dispute over Greenland, he said no. He still expects the United States to help Europe in a crisis, but argues that Europe must make its own decisions whoever is in the White House.
items.cav: Rasmussen’s views are his own. Comments attributed to Frederiksen, Sikorski and Kushner are reported second-hand in the article. Zelenskyy’s account dates from late October, and the sources do not say whether the missile approvals have since been granted.
items.op: Europe’s leverage over Ukraine’s future will come from coordinated decisions, not petitions. Leaders who call Moscow without consulting their partners undercut that position. Influence built on unity is the only kind likely to outlast shifts in Washington.

items.t: Lawyers for Rui Pinto open talks with UK authorities on possible cooperation deal
items.s: The legal team of Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto is negotiating with British authorities about a deal that could see him help uncover financial and sporting crime in the UK. The Serious Fraud Office has reportedly made the first approach.
p: Lawyers for Rui Pinto are holding discussions with British authorities on a possible cooperation arrangement. Under it, the man known as the Manchester City whistleblower would help investigators look into serious financial and sporting wrongdoing in the UK, according to the Guardian.

The Guardian says it obtained information showing that the Serious Fraud Office reached out to Pinto after word spread that he was ready to support British investigators, provided he received protection in return. William Bourdon, a lawyer for Pinto who has also acted for Edward Snowden and Julian Assange, confirmed to the newspaper that contact had been made. He said the process was moving forward but gave no further specifics.

Pinto, who is 38, gathered tens of millions of sensitive files between 2015 and 2019. If a deal is struck, he could become a major source for inquiries into financial crime linked to football, law firms and powerful business figures. He might also help officials spot possible tax offences and other irregularities that could otherwise escape detection.

The bulk of the material is currently held by French authorities, who had earlier tried to bring him into a witness protection scheme. Those plans were derailed when Portuguese police arrested him in Hungary in January 2019, yet France has kept in touch with him.

His own position in Portugal is also in doubt. On 30 September he was told that state protection would end after six years. Officials said there was no danger to his life, but advised him to stay out of public debate on contentious topics, avoid crowded places and limit time with relatives. The move was put on hold once it became clear he had never been able to contest it, and he has lodged an appeal that is still pending.

Pinto’s disclosures have reached into Cristiano Ronaldo’s tax affairs, the proposed breakaway European Super League and a number of contested financial deals. Documents he leaked later fed into the Premier League’s inquiry into Manchester City, which concluded the club had breached financial rules.

In 2023 a Portuguese court handed him a suspended four-year prison sentence for attempted extortion and cybercrime. Two years later he was cleared in a second case with similar charges. The public prosecutor and Benfica, one of the clubs he hacked, have challenged that acquittal, and a higher court has yet to rule. Pinto’s backers describe him as a whistleblower who exposed corruption, while his critics say his methods broke legal and ethical norms. He was also the source behind Luanda Leaks, which laid bare the business empire of Isabel dos Santos, who has denied corruption allegations.
items.cav: The deal is still under negotiation and its terms are unknown. Bourdon gave no details, and the Guardian’s account rests on information it obtained rather than on an official announcement. The outcome of Pinto’s protection appeal and the Portuguese challenge to his acquittal remain pending.
items.op: A whistleblower who may help expose wrongdoing should not be left at the mercy of shifting protection decisions. Portugal’s decision to end Pinto’s protection without first giving him a chance to respond undermines trust in the system. Any British agreement must be transparent and bound by clear rules.

items.t: Oil falls to lowest since August as Trump says Iran war is “effectively over”
items.s: Crude prices slid to their weakest point since late August, lifting European and London equities, after President Donald Trump played down the chance of new strikes on Iran. Airlines and other fuel-sensitive shares led the gains.
p: Brent, the international benchmark, dropped almost 3% to $89.66 in early Tuesday trading, its cheapest level since 31 August. The decline followed a slump of roughly 6% the previous day, which traders linked to signs that the fighting could be winding down.

Speaking at the White House, Trump argued that Israel and Gulf partners were adequately shielded from Iranian threats and that there was no need to escalate. He said military action “doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing” at present, while adding that American forces remained ready to act for any reason.

Across Europe the Stoxx 600 rose 0.9% to 662.54, close to the peak it touched in early August amid hopes of a Middle East settlement. The FTSE 100 in London added 0.4% to 10,828. Carriers gained as investors anticipated lower fuel costs, with Lufthansa up 1.8% and Air France-KLM up 1.2%. Oil majors BP and Shell were the weakest large stocks, falling 1.7% and 1.5%.

Analyst Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com said markets were extending their recovery after a strong session on Wall Street, but warned that underlying economic and corporate risks had not disappeared. She suggested the Federal Reserve would want further evidence of cooling inflation before changing course. The latest US inflation figures for October were due at 1.30pm GMT.
For motorists, the AA reported on Monday that the average UK petrol price had dropped 5p a litre since early October, to 169.7p, and that wholesale prices pointed to a further 10p cut on the way.
items.cav: The account relies on a market report whose summary is partly cut off, so the wider state of the Iran conflict is not fully clear. Trump’s “effectively over” remark is his own characterisation, and the sources do not show whether any formal end to hostilities has been agreed. The petrol price outlook is the AA’s projection, not a confirmed outcome.
items.op: Falling oil prices are welcome, but investors and voters should not mistake a presidential remark for a settled peace. Governments that talk down the risk of strikes owe the public clear, verifiable terms. Until those exist, markets are pricing hope, and that is a fragile basis for a recovery.

items.t: Trump says Iran war is ‘effectively over’ as Tehran denies planned talks with Washington
items.s: US President Donald Trump said there was momentum toward ending the war with Iran, while keeping open the possibility of new strikes. Tehran denied that any meeting with US officials was being planned.
p: On Monday, at a White House briefing, Trump argued that Iran had been largely defeated militarily, describing it as “effectively over”. He said Washington was content to hold the current position for now, but warned that the US could resume attacks if needed, and he judged such strikes to be unlikely.

Trump met Qatar’s Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, whom he described as a key mediator in the conflict. It was the first time he had received a foreign leader since his party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections. Afterwards, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the pair had a productive exchange covering Iran at length.

Trump said Gulf states favoured the present situation over military action, calling the American pressure on Iran a historic naval blockade and pointing to a land operation known as Iron Gate. According to the Euronews report, Iron Gate is a CENTCOM task force that aims to stop advanced weapons, sanctioned goods and illicit money from moving across Iran’s land frontiers and the Caspian Sea. Trump also said all parties accept that Iran must not acquire nuclear arms.

Qatar’s prime minister, who also met Vice President JD Vance in Washington, called the discussions positive. He said the sides had considered how to move forward on negotiations between Washington and Tehran, and he voiced appreciation for progress toward a deal and regional peace.

Iranian officials responded defiantly. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X that the US was thrashing about in desperation and urged Washington to drop what he called invented reports of talks. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said no such meeting was in preparation. Citing a senior security official, the Tasnim news agency reported that Tehran’s negotiating stance had not shifted and that it would not engage with the US until Washington took concrete steps against Iran’s seven demands.

Media reports on Monday, relaying remarks from Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, said Qatar would host a Vance–Rezaei meeting the following week, which Kalin presented as a chance for a real breakthrough. These claims rest on his account and have not been confirmed by the parties. Meanwhile, Iranian authorities said strikes were still hitting targets, including the island of Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz. The US military has not publicly confirmed these strikes. Brent crude futures dropped to $92 a barrel on Monday as traders bet the conflict might soon end.
items.cav: The reported Vance–Rezaei meeting comes only from Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin as relayed by media, and Iran has denied it. The strikes in Iran are reported by Iranian authorities; the US military has not publicly acknowledged them. Trump’s claim that Iran is militarily “effectively over” is his own assessment and is not independently verified in these sources.
items.op: Claims that a war is nearly over sit uneasily beside strikes the US military has not publicly acknowledged. Transparency about where force is used, and which talks are really under way, is the least the public is owed before anyone declares victory. Until Washington and Tehran put verifiable facts on the record, optimism should be treated as a hypothesis, not a settlement.

items.t: Trump calls fresh US strikes on Iran ‘highly unlikely’ but says Washington stays ready to act
items.s: President Donald Trump has said renewed American attacks on Iran are improbable, while warning that US forces remain prepared if conditions change. He made the comments after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, amid mounting domestic pressure over the war.
p: Speaking in the White House briefing room on Monday, Trump argued that Iran’s military had been largely neutralised, and said talks aimed at ending the Middle East conflict were moving in a constructive direction. He described Washington’s current posture as a holding pattern, which he said was being maintained largely at the urging of neighbouring states.

The remarks followed an Oval Office meeting with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani. Trump called the talk a productive exchange about bringing the war to a close. Qatar, a US partner in the Gulf and one of Iran’s neighbours, has played a central mediating role. In a message posted on X, the Qatari leader said he had held constructive discussions with Trump and Vice-President JD Vance about a settlement for the region.

Iranian officials have repeatedly questioned Trump’s earlier suggestions that the conflict was close to resolution. According to the BBC, this is not the first time he has described the war as over in military terms, but his political situation has shifted since then. Diplomacy has largely been conducted through intermediaries since the fighting began after joint US and Israeli strikes in February.

The change in tone follows a difficult set of midterm results for the Republicans last week, which senior party figures, including Vance, attributed in part to the war. Before the vote, Trump had acknowledged limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast on Sunday, he said he saw no current justification for escalating.

Asked why he had not formally declared the war at an end, Trump said some Gulf partners could still be exposed to Iranian aggression. He suggested that the American naval blockade of Iranian ports was helping to make the region safer. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have all been struck by Iranian fire during the conflict, and the threat of attacks has caused significant disruption to air travel in the region.

Energy markets responded to the developments. Oil prices have dropped sharply since the midterms and fell further after Trump’s remarks. On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude traded more than 1% lower at $91.50 a barrel, while US-traded crude was down 1.2% at $85.82.

The fallout is also reaching the Pentagon. Republican Congressman Thomas Massie intends to bring a House vote this week on impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war. Hegseth, who has Trump’s backing, says he is unconcerned by the threat and Trump has dismissed Massie’s push as a stunt. Because Republicans still hold Congress until January, the motion is unlikely to pass, although Democrats have indicated they would support impeachment once the new session starts.
items.cav: The central claims about Iran’s military position and the state of negotiations come from Trump’s own statements, and Iranian officials have disputed his earlier assessments. The account relies on a single outlet, and the sources do not say what terms a deal might involve or when one could be reached.
items.op: A declaration that a war is effectively over is not the same as ending one, especially when allies and markets remain exposed. Washington owes the public a clear account of what has been agreed, what remains open and who answers for the campaign. Leaders who keep the state of war vague should expect scrutiny from Congress and voters.

items.t: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, under investigation, lobbied Trump on China chip exports, BBC analysis says
items.s: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang is being investigated over an affair involving an alleged Chinese spy, according to BBC analysis by Faisal Islam, who argues he matters more to the future of the world order than other tech leaders. Nvidia shares fell about 4% on Monday.
p: In a BBC News analysis, Faisal Islam compares Jensen Huang with the late Steve Jobs, noting that both are admired innovators with a strong personal presence. Huang, however, is now under investigation over an affair involving an alleged Chinese spy, a matter the piece treats as a serious new risk for the company.

The column explains why Nvidia matters so much. The most advanced systems of today depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years those have been produced by Nvidia, using technology that grew out of graphics hardware and manufacturing capacity in Taiwan. Islam writes that the names of its chips mean little to the public, yet they power the technology that is transforming the world.

Islam met Huang in September last year, during Donald Trump’s state visit to the UK. At the time, Huang was pressing the US government to lift export bans on some of the most capable chips sold to China, including the H200. Islam suggested that Huang was one of the few people who could meet Trump at the White House and then Xi Jinping in Beijing within days. Huang said he believed he had persuaded Trump of his case.

Huang argued that the contest between the US and China is not zero-sum and that American interests were better served if the world relied on US technology. He also said that such computing technology was not a national security concern. Islam notes that many people in national security circles reject this view. They argue that the race for the most advanced technology is effectively zero-sum and that the West, and the US in particular, must act to slow Chinese progress.

The column links those public arguments to the current inquiry. It says the period in which Huang was lobbying is now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage. The piece does not set out the scope of that investigation, who is conducting it, or what it has found so far.

Islam reports that Nvidia shares fell about 4% on Monday, which he attributes to new risks at the point where technology and global politics meet. He says the company is still expected to perform strongly, citing hard revenues of about $400bn this year and a market value of more than $4 trillion.
items.cav: This is an analysis column rather than a news report, and the investigation’s details, the identity of the alleged spy and the status of any findings are not in the source. The revenue and valuation figures are reported without a stated original source, and Huang’s claims are his own, relayed second-hand by Islam.
items.op: Huang’s influence over the chips that shape the future of technology is a matter of public interest, and so is how the inquiry into him is handled. Allegations of espionage against a figure with this much reach call for clear, timely disclosure of what is being examined and why, not market rumour. Until findings are public, the presumption of innocence must hold, and investors and governments deserve facts.

items.t: Trump says FBI is looking into Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.s: US President Donald Trump said the FBI is looking into the relationship between Nvidia’s chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy, as Nvidia’s shares fell. Beijing has rejected the claims.
p: Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI was investigating the affair between Jensen Huang, the boss of chipmaker Nvidia, and a woman US authorities allege is a Chinese spy. Trump said he had spoken to Huang that day and asked him whether he knew the woman was a spy. According to Trump, Huang said he had no idea. Trump said he believed him, though he gave few details of the FBI inquiry and did not say when it had begun. The BBC has contacted the FBI, and the bureau’s response was not reported in the evidence.

The woman is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, who the New York Times reported is a managing director of Megaspeed, a Singaporean company that has had dealings with Nvidia. Citing US intelligence officials, the newspaper said they believe she was spying for Beijing. It also reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to senior officials last spring warning about the relationship. These claims come from the newspaper’s reporting and have not been independently confirmed in the evidence. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related.

China’s foreign ministry rejected the allegations that Huang was targeted, calling them groundless and speculative. Nvidia has said it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security had been compromised, and it has launched an internal investigation. In an email to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted the affair, said he was sorry for hurting his wife and children, and pledged to cooperate with the company’s probe.

Several congressional committees have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s security protocols and his dealings with Megaspeed’s executive. It is unclear whether he will attend. The BBC has contacted Nvidia and the committees, and neither had responded in the reporting provided.

Support for Huang has come from some prominent figures in technology and finance. Elon Musk and investors including Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman publicly defended him, with Maguire describing the affair as a serious mistake and Ackman saying Huang should not get a free pass. Trump also said he believed Huang would stay on as chief executive.

Markets reacted sharply. Nvidia shares fell 4.2 per cent on Monday, closing at their lowest level since 7 April, as investors questioned Huang’s future. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies and is central to the current tech boom, and its chips are at the heart of US export restrictions on sales to China. The company’s standing with regulators and lawmakers may now depend on what the FBI and Congress find.
items.cav: The FBI inquiry is confirmed only by Trump’s own remarks, and the evidence gives no details of its scope. The claims that Alice Huang spied for Beijing rely on unnamed US officials as reported by the New York Times, and China denies them. Huang’s account of the affair comes through his email and Trump’s retelling of their call.
items.op: Public officials should not be the only source of assurances in a matter touching national security and US export policy. Trump’s word that Huang is honest is not an investigation. Transparency from the FBI, Nvidia and Congress is what will show whether the chip industry’s most important company was truly safe.

items.t: Trump says US war in Iran is ‘effectively over’ and escalation is not needed
items.s: Donald Trump has described the war in Iran as “effectively over”, downplaying fears that Washington would step up its military campaign against Tehran once the midterm elections were done.
p: Donald Trump has told reporters that the conflict with Iran has essentially ended, pushing back against expectations that the United States would intensify its campaign after the midterms, according to The Guardian.

Speaking at a White House press conference, Trump argued that Israel and Gulf allies were well shielded from Iranian threats and that new strikes were not necessary for now. He nonetheless said American forces were positioned and prepared to act for any reason.

His comments came after a meeting in the Oval Office with the Qatari prime minister, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. Qatar has joined other Gulf states in urging Washington not to restart hostilities. The Guardian reports that the Qatari leader spoke of progress toward ending the conflict within a short timeframe, though the summary does not make clear whether that remark was his or Trump’s.
The outlet also points out that Trump has repeatedly suggested a final peace agreement was close, doing so dozens of times over a war that has now lasted close to nine months.

US troop deployments to the region continued in the weeks before the vote. Some commentators speculated that the administration was holding off on renewed fighting until after the ballot to avoid a political backlash. Republicans then suffered a heavy defeat, losing control of both chambers of Congress, and Vice-President JD Vance publicly blamed the Iran war as a major factor.

Earlier in the day, Trump posted on Truth Social that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait would favour keeping the current arrangement, which he described as a long-running naval blockade. He reiterated that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon and said Washington could return to full-scale operations if conditions changed, while calling such a move unlikely.
items.cav: This account rests on a single outlet, and the sources do not describe the negotiations, the terms under discussion or conditions on the ground. It is also unclear from the summary whether the “fairly soon” remark came from Trump or from the Qatari prime minister, although the headline attributes it to Trump.
items.op: A claim that the war is “effectively over” should be tested against facts, not applause, especially from a leader who has repeatedly predicted an imminent deal. Before the public accepts that fighting has ended, the administration should set out plainly what has been agreed, what remains unresolved, and what would trigger renewed strikes. Transparency is the only real test.

items.t: Republican congressman moves to force House impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
items.s: Representative Thomas Massie plans to bring impeachment articles against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to a House vote this week, a step widely expected to fail. Massie says his aim is to prompt President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats take control of Congress.
p: Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky formally filed articles of impeachment against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor on Monday, according to the BBC. He accuses Hegseth of breaching the US Constitution.

Massie argues that Hegseth has been waging hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without authorisation from Congress, and says that makes the defence secretary answerable under the law. Asked why he was pressing ahead, Massie told reporters he was acting on principle.

Few observers expect the effort to succeed, since Republicans keep their majorities until January. Massie's stated goal is to push Trump into dismissing Hegseth before Democrats can open an impeachment inquiry of their own.

Hegseth struck a dismissive tone. He said he was unconcerned, and told reporters he would hold a news conference on Tuesday morning on the subject. The BBC notes that his previous news conference took place in May.

Massie lost his re-election bid earlier this year. He has been a vocal critic of Trump and of the Iran conflict, which began almost nine months ago, and he has also pressed the administration to release federal files on Jeffrey Epstein. The articles, as reported, accuse Hegseth of intimidating critics of the administration, of seizing foreign leaders and of disregarding War Powers resolutions. The BBC did not independently verify these allegations.

Once the resolution is filed, House Speaker Mike Johnson has to set a date to take it up within two days. Members may vote on it outright, send it to committee, or shelve it. House Democrats look likely to support it, and their leader Hakeem Jeffries said he would be a firm supporter. Massie himself said he was unsure there were enough votes to pass it.

Peter Loge, a public affairs professor at George Washington University, told the BBC that the measure could clear the House because the Republican margin is so narrow, and that some frustrated Republicans may stay away from the vote. Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University, said impeachment has become more frequent as American politics has grown more polarised, and predicted several more of Trump's cabinet members could face it.

Removing a cabinet secretary requires approval by both chambers. The House has impeached only two cabinet members in US history, and the Senate convicted neither. A conviction needs two-thirds of senators, a bar Democrats would not reach in January without Republican votes. Gowder suggested the current Senate could confirm a replacement if Hegseth left before the new session, while Loge said Hegseth's chances of serving out Trump's term are slim.
items.cav: The allegations are Massie's claims as set out in the articles, and the BBC report does not confirm them. Hegseth's only response in the sources is that he is unconcerned, and the content of his planned news conference is not described. The expected outcome is also contested, as Loge expects the House to pass the measure while Massie is unsure it has the votes.
items.op: Serious accusations against a cabinet secretary deserve a full, transparent process, not a rushed vote aimed at getting ahead of a rival party. Congress should test the claims on the record, and Trump should explain publicly how he will address the questions the articles raise.

items.t: Steel plant blast in western Turkey kills at least 17 workers
items.s: At least 17 people have died and more were hurt after an explosion and fire at an iron and steel plant in Aliaga, near Izmir in western Turkey. Officials say the blast followed a crane accident during work at the site.
p: The explosion happened around midday at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, a port district of Izmir province. According to the BBC, the victims were all workers at the facility, one of Turkey’s leading steel producers. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the plant and a tall column of smoke.

The Izmir governor, Süleyman Elban, said a crane carrying a replacement boiler had collapsed, sending materials into a furnace below. Euronews, citing President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s televised address, reported the same sequence. The company that runs the plant said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance on one of its electric arc furnaces.

Casualty figures have shifted. Erdoğan first put the death toll at 16. Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu later said one critically injured person had died, raising the total to 17.
