The number of injured is reported differently: the BBC gives 12, while Euronews gives 13, including two in critical condition.

Elban told reporters that some people were believed to still be trapped under the rubble, and search and rescue work continued. Izmir mayor Cemil Tugay said on X that teams were working to remove the collapsed platform.

Erdoğan confirmed the deaths after a cabinet meeting and said investigations were under way. He said the circumstances, including whether there was negligence and who bears responsibility, would be established. The BBC’s Turkish service, citing local media, reported that at least five people had been arrested. Those arrests have not been confirmed by the authorities in the sources available.

The Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society group, said workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey. Euronews described the Habas group as privately owned, and said the plant was founded in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel a year, according to the company’s website. That capacity figure comes from the company itself and has not been independently verified in these reports.
items.cav: The sources differ on the number of injured (12 or 13) and on the arrests, which rest on local media reports relayed by the BBC. The cause is described by officials and the company, and the investigation has not yet reported findings.
items.op: When workers die in an industrial blast, the public is owed a clear account of who inspected the equipment and who approved the work. Investigators should publish their findings, and any negligence should be answered for under the law, not left to a statement of regret.

items.t: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang admits affair as board opens national security probe
items.s: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted an affair after reports that he may have been targeted by a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The company’s board has launched an independent investigation, and analysts say his position could be at risk.
p: For more than three decades, Jensen Huang has been the public face of Nvidia, which he co-founded in 1993 and grew into one of the most valuable chipmakers in the world. He has also kept the company close to his family, with his children Madison and Spencer holding senior roles and his wife, Lori Mills Huang, running the family foundation, which is reported to control more than 60 million Nvidia shares as of 2024.

That image was badly damaged this weekend. The New York Times reported at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset with whom he had developed a close relationship. In a letter to employees on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that he had been having an affair.

The Times reported that US officials had suspected Huang of helping to smuggle American chips into China and had monitored Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean datacentre firm Megaspeed. According to the reporting, officials allegedly concluded during that surveillance that she was a Chinese spy and had become close to the Nvidia leader. Earlier, a company spokesperson had said there was nothing out of the ordinary about his interactions with her. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment before publication.

In his letter, Huang said he supported the investigation, wrote that he took full responsibility for the hurt he had caused, and apologised to his family. Nvidia’s board has now launched an independent inquiry into the national security concerns linked to the relationship.

Analysts and investors quoted in the report said Huang could be removed as chief executive depending on the outcome. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives described it as a “black eye moment” that could prompt congressional inquiries and weigh on the share price. Ken Mahoney of Mahoney Asset Management compared Huang’s role at Nvidia to that of Steve Jobs at Apple, while warning that the bigger question was whether a successor could keep the company’s strategic direction.

Nvidia shares fell 7.5% at the opening of the market, wiping out more than $330bn in value, according to the report. Andy Challenger of Challenger, Gray & Christmas argued that the case was about judgment and national security exposure, not only personal morality.

In a statement, the board said it did not believe national security or company secrets had been compromised, and it expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team, while promising further updates as appropriate.
items.cav: The account of the alleged spy and surveillance comes from New York Times reporting as relayed by the Guardian, and the Guardian did not independently confirm it. Megaspeed had not responded, and the board’s finding that no secrets were compromised is a preliminary statement, not the outcome of the investigation. The talk of Huang’s possible removal is analysts’ speculation.
items.op: A company’s leadership should not hinge on one executive’s private life, but when that life touches a national security inquiry, shareholders and the public are owed more than reassurance. The board’s independent investigation should be published in full, with its findings open to scrutiny. Confidence statements are no substitute for transparency.

items.t: Nvidia shares fall after board opens investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.s: Nvidia’s share price dropped about 4% on Monday after the chipmaker’s board said it would investigate chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman US officials reportedly believe was a Chinese spy. Beijing has rejected the claims.
p: Nvidia’s market value fell sharply on Monday, with the stock down roughly 4% at the close, after the company said its board would run an independent inquiry into chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The BBC put the loss in market value at about $250bn (£190bn).

The probe followed press reports suggesting Washington believed Huang had been singled out in a Chinese espionage effort. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair, calling himself “unfaithful” and apologising to his wife and children. He said he remained committed to protecting the company and supporting US national security, and pledged to cooperate. Nvidia said it had no reason to think its secrets or national security had been compromised.

According to a New York Times report cited by the BBC, American intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, worked for Beijing. She ran Singapore-based Megaspeed, a firm that has done business with Nvidia. The same account says Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to senior officials last spring, cautioning that the chief executive had a close bond with a Chinese agent. The BBC noted that these assertions are not independently verified in the material it had.

Beijing has dismissed the accusations, with its foreign ministry calling them baseless and designed to besmirch China. On Capitol Hill, members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee have asked Huang to attend a private briefing about his contacts with Alice Huang and about how Nvidia guards against espionage. Three lawmakers, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, wrote that the reports raise serious concerns about Chinese access to sensitive American technology and that Congress must establish how far national security may have been put at risk.

Other prominent tech executives, Elon Musk among them, have publicly backed Huang remaining in charge. Analysts quoted by the BBC expected the setback to fade. Victoria Fernandez of Crossmark Global Investments said investors were unlikely to desert a company so vital to the sector building hardware for emerging technologies, though she noted Nvidia has no obvious heir to Huang.

Governance is the sharper question. The BBC reported Huang holds only about 3.5% of the company, and because Nvidia has a single class of voting shares, that stake would not give him a veto over a board decision to remove him. That contrasts with founders such as Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, who hold substantial stakes across several share classes. Fernandez doubted the board would move against Huang without clear evidence of wrongdoing linked to national security or intellectual property, though she expected a possible number two to be identified. Savers are also exposed: pensions and savings in index-tracking funds holding Nvidia can move with its share price.
items.cav: The affair and the espionage claims come from a New York Times report that the BBC relayed, and the sources do not show independent confirmation of Alice Huang’s alleged role. China has denied the allegations, and Nvidia has not said what the investigation will examine or when it will report.
items.op: A chief executive’s private conduct is his own business, but when it may intersect with alleged espionage, shareholders and lawmakers have a legitimate claim to facts. Nvidia’s inquiry should be genuinely independent and its findings published in full. Investors should not be reassured by a share price rebound; transparency must decide whether Huang stays.

items.t: Massie pushes for a House impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
items.s: Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie has filed eight articles of impeachment against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, opening the way for a possible House vote this week. The step follows months of criticism of Hegseth over the Iran war and other military operations.
p: Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman from Kentucky who is leaving office and has frequently clashed with President Donald Trump, has pressed for a House vote to remove Pete Hegseth. According to The Guardian, Massie charges that the defense secretary waged war without congressional approval and misused the authority of his office.

Speaking on the House floor, Massie told colleagues that Hegseth had committed “high crimes and misdemeanors” and had carried out unlawful orders. The Guardian reports that Massie is expected to attract some Republican votes. Under House rules, a vote would have to be held by Wednesday at the latest.

Massie first filed the articles on 15 September. Speaker Mike Johnson then adjourned Congress before the measure could be considered. Republicans will keep their House majority until newly elected members are sworn in during January.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House who is widely tipped to become speaker, has described himself as a “hard yes” on impeachment. In an interview with ABC News on Sunday, he said Hegseth needs to leave his post.

On Monday, Hegseth addressed the Naval War College and unveiled changes to military training, arguing they would help officers wage war swiftly and with deadly precision. Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other Republican figures have blamed their heavy losses in last week’s midterm elections largely on the Iran conflict and its impact on household finances.

Hegseth answered his critics in a brief video posted on Thursday, calling the impeachment push an attempt at personal ruin and saying it would fail against him. The watchdog groups Common Cause and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington contend that the video breaches the Hatch Act, which limits the use of public money for partisan purposes.

Massie’s resolution lays out further charges. It asserts that Hegseth bypassed Congress’s constitutional power to declare war through unauthorised strikes on Iran and Yemen. It also cites the deaths of more than 100 children at a school in Iran and accuses him of ordering suspected drug boats in the Caribbean sunk without rescuing their crews. The document further contends that the investigation and threatened prosecution of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, over calls for troops to refuse illegal orders, violated the First Amendment, and it describes the alleged kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro as unlawful.
items.cav: The sources do not confirm whether the House vote will happen or how many Republicans will support it. The allegations, including the claim about child deaths in Iran and the legality of the Maduro operation, come from Massie’s resolution and are not independently established in the reporting.
items.op: Impeachment is a grave remedy and should turn on whether an official broke the law, not on who is politically inconvenient. If Congress believes Hegseth acted without authorisation, it should weigh the evidence in public and vote on the record. Delaying the question again would tell voters that accountability depends on party loyalty.

items.t: Jensen Huang’s affair raises questions about Trump’s response to intelligence warnings
items.s: The Nvidia co-founder has admitted an affair with a Chinese businesswoman said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. The Guardian’s editorial board argues that the White House’s failure to act on warnings demands an explanation.
p: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman. According to the Guardian, she is said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. The paper describes the case as something close to a spy thriller, given Huang’s status as one of the most powerful figures in the technology boom.

According to the editorial, Donald Trump was briefed on the relationship and took no action. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “No, I don’t think so.” The paper suggests that he may have seen the matter as a private breach of marriage vows, or that he chose to overlook it.

The editorial links the episode to Nvidia’s growing influence in Washington. Huang is described as a backer of Trump’s datacentre expansion, a donor to the White House ballroom project, and an ally in opposing safeguards on the technology. The Guardian says Nvidia’s chips, which became central to the race for tech supremacy, also became a national security issue once China joined the competition.

The paper recounts that the US imposed export controls on GPU sales to China in October 2022, and that Nvidia was effectively barred from selling to Beijing about thirty months later. It says Huang lobbied for looser rules, and that the White House then scrapped Biden-era global chip restrictions and allowed sales of Nvidia’s H200 processors to Chinese customers.

The Guardian reports that Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company whose executive was Ms Huang, was investigated in 2025 over suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. Analysts at Culper Research argued in May that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenue, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. The editorial also says that more than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation once Wall Street opened.

According to the paper, reports suggest the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia contacted investigators. The editorial says Democrats, encouraged by their midterm success, are likely to seek answers, and that Congress has grounds to examine whether the administration knowingly set aside a foreign intelligence threat.

The editorial places the case within a longer history. It notes that diplomatic or military honeytraps have traditionally been more common than commercial ones, and that British intelligence agencies accused Beijing in 2008 of using sex to pressure businesses. The paper states that whether this has happened in the Huang case is unknown.
items.cav: This is an editorial opinion, and its account of the intelligence claims is second-hand: the paper says Alice Huang is “said to have” passed intelligence to Beijing. The report that the commerce probe was halted rests on unnamed reports, and the editorial does not confirm whether any honeytrap took place.
items.op: Whether a chipmaker’s lobbying shaped national security policy is a question of public trust, not partisanship. If the president knew of a possible security risk and chose inaction while easing export rules, Washington owes the public a full and transparent explanation.

items.t: Nvidia shares fall as investigation opens into reports CEO was targeted by Chinese intelligence
items.s: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation after reports that chief executive Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, a claim China denies. Shares fell in premarket trading as the story spread.
p: Nvidia said it was launching an independent investigation following reports that its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been the target of “a foreign intelligence effort”. According to the reports, that effort led to a romantic relationship between Huang and a Chinese woman, Alice Huang, who had allegedly been recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Huang has admitted an affair. In a statement he said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family. He also said he was “fully committed to Nvidia” and would work to earn back employees’ confidence. China has denied the spying claims.

Alice Huang reportedly worked for Megaspeed, a datacentre company based in Singapore. Megaspeed has been suspected of routing Nvidia chips to China and evading export controls, though the reporting cited in the evidence does not establish that as fact. Jensen Huang has publicly criticised US export controls on advanced chips, arguing in May 2025 that they had been a failure.

The Financial Times reported that Alice Huang and a business partner, Kang Wei, sought investment in early 2025 for a south-east Asian data centre project worth several hundred million dollars. According to two investors, the pair said they had “no problem securing GPUs” and cited Alibaba as a client. A US hedge fund had claimed six months earlier that Alibaba secretly funded Megaspeed.

Markets reacted quickly. Nvidia ended last week worth $4.5tn, and shares were down around 6% in premarket trading, with more than $200bn potentially wiped from its value once Wall Street opened. Asian markets were recovering, with Japan’s Nikkei up 2.2% and Taiwan’s TAIEX up almost 5%. Elon Musk publicly backed a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that criticised Huang’s conduct.

Separately, Bloomberg reported that Alphabet is rolling out a broader range of its tensor processing units, custom chips used to develop and run software, which adds to competitive pressure on Nvidia. Prediction market Polymarket put the chance of Huang resigning or being removed by the end of the year at 15%.
items.cav: The espionage link rests on reports and claims, not on any confirmed finding, and the investigation’s outcome is not yet known. The Alibaba funding claim comes from a hedge fund’s allegation made months earlier, and the investor accounts are second-hand. Market figures are premarket and may change.
items.op: Whatever the facts of this affair, the public interest is in an independent inquiry that is transparent about its findings. Nvidia’s investors and the wider public deserve clear answers on export controls and on who was able to reach its chief executive. Speculation should not substitute for evidence.

items.t: Cop31 opens in Antalya as UN warns heat is building faster and the US stays away
items.s: Climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, opened as the World Meteorological Organization reported that heat is building up in Earth's systems at a faster pace. The United States, which has withdrawn from the international climate framework, will again send no official delegation.
p: The UN’s weather agency said the gap between the energy Earth receives from the sun and the energy it sends back has reached its largest level since measurements began. Releasing its global climate update as the summit got under way, it said 2026 was on course to rank among the four hottest years ever recorded.

According to the agency, average surface temperatures from January to September 2026 ran about 1.47C above the preindustrial level. Monthly sea surface temperature records were broken, and sea levels stood at their highest since record-keeping started. Oceans take in roughly 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases, and 2026 is on track to be the tenth straight year of record ocean heat.

The agency warned that this heat build-up will intensify extreme weather, including heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the world had moved into an era of severe climate extremes, pointing to a strong El Niño event layered on top of human-caused warming. He added that the people who have done least to cause the problem are suffering most.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister, is presiding over the negotiations in Antalya. Our colleague Adam Morton questioned him about the apparent contradictions in Australia’s record: a country with high emissions is leading the talks while still exporting fossil fuels and approving projects that add pollution.

Young activists at the summit also made their case. Janiely Truká, an Indigenous activist and poet from Brazil who advises Unicef Brazil on youth issues, said that for Indigenous communities the climate crisis threatens their way of life, their traditional knowledge and their future generations. She called for firm funding commitments, protection of Indigenous territories and easier access for young people to these negotiations.

The United States will again have no official government presence at the summit, the second year running. A White House official said the administration would not send anyone and criticised the summit for ignoring what it sees as the damage done by extreme climate policies. About 20 members of Congress travelling to Antalya have been refused the usual State Department support and are relying on philanthropic money. Democratic congressman Sean Casten, who is attending, described the situation as outrageous.

A recent UN report found that the US was the one major economy that did not cut or slow its carbon pollution last year, adding an extra 133m tons of planet-warming gases from coal, oil and gas. President Donald Trump has previously dismissed climate action as a scam. Finance is expected to be the most contentious issue, with developing countries pressing for money that wealthier nations would rather keep off the agenda.
items.cav: The temperature and ocean figures come from a World Meteorological Organization update covering only January to September, so they are provisional. Several claims about the US and the summit come from live coverage and from quotes given by officials and lawmakers, and the sources do not independently verify them. The article does not say what outcomes the talks are likely to produce.
items.op: Transparency at these summits matters as much as ambition. Delegates should publish agendas and funding arrangements early, and governments that talk about climate finance should show the money. Vague promises from any capital, including the host, will not protect the people already paying the price.

items.t: Kraków shooting: Polish prosecutors widen probe as attacker dies in hospital
items.s: Six people were killed when a gunman opened fire in Kraków’s main square over the weekend, and the 24-year-old Polish attacker has since died in hospital. Authorities say the investigation will continue to determine whether he acted alone.
p: Polish investigators opened a terrorism case after a gunman from Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a town in southeastern Poland, fired on people in the city’s central square on Saturday afternoon, according to the Guardian’s live coverage. Six people lost their lives, one of them a Briton, and 17 others were wounded. Authorities later said the assailant, who had been hit during an exchange of fire with officers, died in hospital.

A national day of mourning was declared for the first of two planned days. Police said the bodies of three relatives were found at the attacker’s home: his father, 53, his mother, 52, and his 21-year-old sister. Among the wounded were nationals of Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia, as well as two police officers, one of them in serious condition.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect had been drawn to far-right ideas and held “very radical” views. Those remarks were later softened, and nationalist opposition figures challenged the basis on which they had been made. Government spokesperson Adam Szlapka urged restraint in commenting while the initial signs remained unconfirmed.

According to interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka, Poland’s cybercrime bureau, CBZC, has detained five people over online posts praising the shooter. She warned that officers were on heightened alert for possible copycat attacks.

Justice minister Waldemar Zurek said the probe would proceed despite the attacker’s death, with a focus on whether the gunman worked alone. The square reopened on Sunday evening after the security cordon was removed.
items.cav: The account comes from a live blog that relays official statements and has not been independently verified. The interior minister’s ideological claims were partly walked back and their basis has been disputed, so the suspect’s motive remains unclear. The sources do not say what the five detained people are suspected of or whether the posts led to charges.
items.op: A rare mass shooting in a city centre demands facts, not early labels. Poland’s government was right to pull back from a motive it could not yet support. Transparency now means publishing what the investigation establishes, including whether anyone helped the gunman, and treating the detained suspects with the presumption of innocence.

items.t: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang admits affair as reports link his companion to alleged Chinese spying
items.s: Nvidia's chief executive has admitted an extramarital affair after US media reports said the woman involved was suspected of spying for Beijing. The company has opened an independent investigation.
p: Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the chipmaker Nvidia, has acknowledged an extramarital affair. On Sunday he said he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologised for the hurt caused to her and their children. He also said he would cooperate with an internal security investigation.

The affair is with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman who is not related to him. According to a New York Times report, which the BBC cites, US intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by China’s top intelligence agency and was spying for Beijing. Her current whereabouts are unknown. She did not respond to a request for comment from the newspaper.

Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm that had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia says it investigated those concerns and found them to be unfounded. The BBC understands that Megaspeed is now under investigation by the Singapore government over earlier claims that it evaded US sanctions on exports of Nvidia’s high-end chips.

The New York Times reported that surveillance captured communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was later identified as Jensen Huang. It remains unclear what intelligence, if any, she gathered and passed on. Nvidia told the BBC it was not aware of any intelligence concerns, and said it trusted the US government would have warned it of a genuine threat. China has rejected the allegations as “groundless”.

The reports have a political dimension. According to the New York Times, Donald Trump was briefed last year on intelligence alleging that Alice Huang was spying for China. Asked whether he wished he had acted on it, Trump said he did not think so and called Huang “an honourable guy”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment, though the newspaper reported that he had overseen a memo last spring warning the administration about the relationship.

The stakes are high because Nvidia sits at the centre of the contest between the US and China over the most advanced technology. Export controls introduced since 2022 have largely shut the company out of the Chinese market, and Huang has pursued talks between Washington and Beijing in an effort to win back access. The affair, the reports suggest, may have complicated his hopes of a broader approval to sell more advanced chips to China.
Huang, born in Taiwan in 1963, co-founded Nvidia after working at AMD. Bloomberg’s billionaires index estimates his fortune at $155bn.
items.cav: Much of the espionage detail is second-hand, drawn from a New York Times report that the BBC relayed, and Alice Huang has not commented. What intelligence she may have passed to Beijing is unknown, and Nvidia’s claim that US national security was not compromised has not been independently verified.
items.op: The question is not Huang’s marriage but whether a company central to national security was kept properly informed. Officials who held intelligence about his associate owe lawmakers and the public a clearer account of what was known and what was done. Reassurance from either Nvidia or the administration is no substitute for transparency.

items.t: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about offering Dana White the press secretary job
items.s: President Donald Trump has said he was not serious when he publicly offered the White House press secretary job to Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. The offer had been announced a day earlier.
p: On Sunday, Trump told reporters he had been joking when he announced the offer, according to the BBC. He said White liked the idea but described the invitation as lighthearted.

The offer had been made in a post on Truth Social on Saturday, in which Trump urged White to take the role and predicted he would be unlike any previous press secretary. Trump also said White could bring several current and former mixed martial arts fighters along as aides.
Speaking at a news conference on Saturday, White did not say whether he would accept. He said he already had a lot of commitments and expected to discuss the matter at a meeting with Trump on Monday.

Trump later said White was coming to Washington on Monday for other reasons and that he would meet him there. The Guardian and Al Jazeera also reported Trump’s “kidding” remarks under similar headlines.
The press secretary post has been vacant since October, when Katie Zacharia left after less than five days. She had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who held the job from the start of Trump’s second term.

The episode follows Republican losses in the midterm elections, which cost the party its majority in both houses of Congress. White runs the UFC and PowerSlap, has recently launched the boxing promotion Zuffa Boxing, and sits on the board of Meta. He spoke at Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
items.cav: The detailed account comes from the BBC; the Guardian and Al Jazeera are represented only by short summaries, so their wording is not verified beyond the headlines. Whether White will take any role remains unresolved, and Trump’s Saturday post sits uneasily with his Sunday description of the offer as a joke.
items.op: A press secretary speaks for the government to the public every day, so the appointment deserves a transparent process rather than a social media post later described as a joke. When a public offer is made and then waved off, citizens cannot tell what is real. Voters are owed statements they can take at face value.

items.t: Kraków market square shooting suspect dies in hospital, Polish police say
items.s: A 24-year-old Polish man suspected of killing six people in a shooting in central Kraków has died in hospital, police said on Monday. Investigators are still working to establish his motive.
p: The suspect was wounded in an exchange of fire with police on Saturday and died early on Monday, according to the Lesser Poland police, who announced the death on X. Authorities have not yet officially named him. Doctors had earlier described his condition as critical.

The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time in Kraków’s Main Market Square, a busy area of the Old Town that is usually crowded with tourists. Police said the gunman drove at high speed into the square and fired at random, and that he kept shooting even after being wounded by officers. Armed officers engaged him and he was shot within minutes, officials said.

Police said three bodies were found at the suspect’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town north of Kraków. On Sunday they confirmed the dead were his father, 53, his mother, 52, and his sister, 21. Police said the injuries appeared to be gunshot wounds, and the cause and nature of the deaths are still being clarified.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the gunman was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held radical, ultranationalist views. Prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said it would continue despite the suspect’s death and would aim to establish whether he acted alone. He asked for “restraint” and said evidence would not be disclosed for now.

Six people were killed, four of them Polish, along with an Austrian woman aged 51 and a British man aged 32. Reports differ on the number injured, with most citing 15 or 16. Two police officers were among the wounded, and both were reported to have come out of medically induced comas on Sunday. Two surgeons who were eating nearby treated victims on the street.

The suspect reportedly held a firearms permit. Four firearms, including two AR-15 rifles and two handguns, were found in his car, along with several hundred rounds of ammunition, according to the spokesperson for the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Poland declared two days of national mourning, and flags were lowered to half mast. Mourners left candles in the square, which reopened late on Sunday. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the attack as terrorism, the deadliest in Poland since the end of communism in 1989, according to Euronews.
items.cav: Sources disagree on the number of injured (15 or 16), on the distance from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski to Kraków (about 100 miles or 150 kilometres), and on the gender split of the Polish victims. The motive remains unconfirmed; the early ministerial description has not been backed by released evidence, and details about the permit and the surgeons come from media reports.
items.op: A suspect’s death ends one threat but not the questions. Officials offered early labels for motive before prosecutors said the evidence was still under review. Public trust depends on the terrorism inquiry establishing, in open and checkable terms, who acted, why, and whether anyone else was involved. Those answers, not the speed of the labelling, will decide how this case is remembered.

items.t: Seven dead and more than 100 injured as two trains collide south of Cairo
items.s: Seven people were killed and at least 125 were injured when two passenger trains collided on Sunday in Giza province, Egypt. Rail workers began repairing the damaged track the following day.
p: The crash took place on Sunday near Al-Ayyat, roughly 52 kilometres south of the Egyptian capital, according to Euronews. The Transport Ministry said a northbound-to-Fayoum service ran into the back of a passenger train that was standing still and headed for Aswan. The BBC placed the scene between the Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations and reported that several carriages came off the rails and tumbled down an embankment.

Photographs from the site showed people looking through overturned carriages for anyone still hurt, as a large emergency operation got going. Egypt’s health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, told the BBC that patients were being treated for fractures and head trauma, and that local hospitals had been told to stay prepared for a surge in arrivals. Egypt’s Health Ministry later said more than 70 hurt passengers had left hospital after care.

The BBC reported that the driver of one of the trains was among the dead, a claim it attributed to the ministry. Euronews did not mention this. The Egyptian Red Crescent said its teams were offering relief and emotional help to the injured and their relatives at the scene.

Ahmad Othman Abu Emran, an eyewitness, told Euronews he was working in a field close by when the collision happened. He recalled the force of the impact and the noise of carriages flipping, then ran over to assist, calling what he saw devastating.

President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi has called for an urgent inquiry into what caused the collision. The BBC quoted him as saying that anyone found to have been careless should be held to account. The same outlet reported demands in Egypt that the transport minister step down, though neither report says whether the government has answered those demands.

Euronews said crews, cranes and rail workers were clearing the wreckage and fixing the track on Monday. The BBC noted that services between Giza and Upper Egypt had been halted, and the railway authority had not said how long the stoppage would last. Euronews added that the crash has revived concern about upkeep and management across the country’s rail system, and it recalled a 2002 fire that killed more than 300 people. The BBC put the official toll from that disaster above 370.
items.cav: The sources differ on several points: the injury count (125 versus more than 100), the direction of the trains, and the death toll in the 2002 fire. The claim that the train driver died comes only from the BBC, and the reports on resignation calls are not followed by any official response.
items.op: Egypt’s rail network has faced safety criticism for years, and the families of the dead deserve a clear account of what went wrong. Sisi’s order for an urgent investigation is a start, but accountability depends on publishing the findings and naming any failures. Otherwise the next collision will bring the same grief and the same promises.

items.t: Nvidia opens independent probe into CEO Jensen Huang over affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.s: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang, who has admitted an affair with a woman that US officials reportedly believe was spying for China. The case raises questions for the world's most valuable chipmaker and the wider race for advanced chips.
p: Nvidia’s board said the inquiry was opened in light of recent reporting that Huang had been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” It said it had “no reason to believe” that national security or Nvidia’s secrets were compromised, but that the review would examine all available information. The investigation is being led by independent board members and an external law firm.

In a letter to employees, Huang said he took “full responsibility” for his actions. He said he had been unfaithful to his wife, apologised to his family, and acknowledged that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to employees, the board and shareholders. According to Euronews, the letter did not name the woman involved or her reported ties to Beijing.

The Financial Times first reported the affair. It identified the woman as Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm that has become Nvidia’s largest customer in Southeast Asia. Alice Huang is not related to the CEO, according to the BBC. The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials believed she was working for China’s Ministry of State Security. These claims have not been confirmed publicly by US intelligence officials.

Beijing has rejected the allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the claims were entirely groundless and intended to smear China. Reports said US officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before President Donald Trump travelled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Trump has defended Huang, describing him as a “fine person” and saying he had not spoken to him about the matter. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence sooner, Trump said he did not think so. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment on the matter.

The affair comes as Nvidia, valued at about $5 trillion, faces doubts over the sustainability of a massive spending boom and a sell-off in related stocks. Huang has lobbied Trump to ease chip export restrictions on China, and the sales deal has been slowed by strict licence reviews. Analysts said Huang’s influence could be weakened, and that the company depends heavily on him, with no obvious successor.
items.cav: The espionage claims come from press reports citing US officials, and the officials have not commented publicly. Nvidia’s conclusion that secrets were not compromised is its own view and has not been tested by the investigation. Some details, including the memo and Trump’s briefing, rest on second-hand reporting.
items.op: A chipmaker’s chief executive is not above scrutiny when national security may be at stake. Nvidia’s investigation is a start, but its findings should be made public as far as possible. Shareholders and the public deserve to know whether a foreign power gained access to sensitive technology, not only whether the company is comfortable with its own answer.

items.t: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang faces questions over alleged Chinese espionage link
items.s: Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into whether chief executive Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The allegations centre on a Chinese businesswoman, and the company’s shares fell more than 4 percent in overnight trading.
p: Scrutiny has landed on Nvidia’s chief executive after reports that a Chinese woman he had a romantic involvement with may have been collecting information for Beijing. Huang, who helped found the chipmaker more than thirty years ago, has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife. The firm, however, says it sees no grounds to think sensitive US material or proprietary data has been exposed.

The board has commissioned a review, led by a committee of directors with outside lawyers, to establish whether Huang was the subject of a foreign spying effort. The inquiry followed media coverage tying him to Alice Huang, who previously worked as an executive at a data centre firm based in Singapore. Reports indicate the two are not related, despite sharing a surname. Huang has pledged to cooperate and to keep leading the company.

The claims originated with a New York Times investigation published last month. That outlet cited American intelligence officials who believed Beijing had enlisted Alice Huang to learn about the chief executive and perhaps sway Nvidia’s chip sales into China. Exactly what she obtained, whether anything sensitive reached Chinese hands, and how much Huang understood about any scheme are still unknown.

Huang told Bloomberg News in late October that his dealings with her were tied to Megaspeed, her company, and were ordinary. According to the Times, Megaspeed became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying roughly $4.8bn of equipment. American authorities have reportedly examined Megaspeed since 2024, suspecting it helped China acquire top Nvidia processors despite export controls. No criminal charges against either Huang have been reported.

Alice Huang, also called Huang Le, has not commented on the espionage allegations, and her whereabouts are unknown. An entry in a Chinese investment database lists earlier roles at HSBC and Chinese broadcasters, though AFP said it could not verify those details independently.

Politicians from both major parties are weighing in. Republican members of Congress have asked Huang to appear before lawmakers on 18 November, arguing that China’s possible access to sensitive American technology is at stake. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded answers from the company and urged passage of tougher rules to keep advanced US technology away from China.

Investors reacted quickly, with Nvidia’s market value of $4.5 trillion sliding more than 4 percent in overnight trading into Monday. Chris Beauchamp of IG Group said it was too early to tell whether the episode would prove a “major turning point” for the company.
items.cav: The sources do not establish what information, if any, was passed to Beijing, nor what Huang knew. Much of the espionage account rests on anonymous US intelligence officials as reported by the New York Times, and details of Alice Huang’s background are unverified. Her side of the story has not been heard.
items.op: Allegations of foreign espionage touching a company central to US chip policy are a matter of public interest, not private scandal. The independent review and congressional testimony should be conducted in the open, with findings published. Investors, lawmakers and the public deserve clear answers rather than assurances from the company.

items.t: Four killed in Gaza as sand embankment collapses onto displaced families’ tents after heavy rain
items.s: Four people, including three children, died when a sand embankment fell onto tents at a displaced families’ camp in central Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. The collapse came after heavy rain reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across the territory.
p: The health ministry says a woman and three children were killed on Sunday night when earth piled up in a sand embankment gave way onto tents at a camp south of Deir al-Balah. Five people were reportedly pulled out alive after the collapse.

The disaster followed torrential rain the previous day, which reportedly swamped tens of thousands of tents throughout Gaza and left many displaced Palestinians with nowhere dry to sleep. According to the Civil Defence service, water reached depths of up to 1.5 metres in places, and its responders could attend to just 10% of the 2,100 emergency calls they received.

Footage circulated online showed people searching for survivors by the light of mobile phones, picking through boulders, sand and crushed tents. Mustafa al-Masri, a rescuer, told the BBC that the rescue crews and young men from the camp had to reach the trapped people by hand, because the mound was so large and spread so wide that nobody knew how to start.

The official count has changed. The Civil Defence first said that two women and three children had died, but on Monday morning the health ministry said only one woman was among the dead. The names it has given are Tahrir Nabhan, Mariam Nabhan, her brother Salah and Habiba al-Zein.

The Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, urged international bodies to supply secure shelters and relocate tents away from sandy ground, slopes and any spot prone to collapse. Karl Baker of the International Organization for Migration described the aid now entering Gaza as far too limited, comparing it to the most minimal of plasters and calling for more donations in kind and funding.

Cogat, the Israeli military unit that coordinates aid deliveries, said more than 91,000 tents and other supplies had reached Gaza under its winter preparation scheme. It also said Israel would bar any equipment that Hamas or other armed factions could use for military ends. The UN estimates that roughly 80% of Gaza’s buildings have been destroyed or damaged, and that 1.2 million of the more than 1.9 million displaced people live in tents or improvised shelters.

Masri said he had been forced out of Beit Hanoun in the north but remained in central Gaza, having found no other place he considered suitable. The UN warns that conditions stay grave despite the October 2025 ceasefire, as Israeli strikes keep hitting populated areas.
items.cav: The casualty figures differ between sources: the Civil Defence first reported five deaths, while the health ministry later reported four, and the sources do not explain the revision in detail. Both the health ministry and the Civil Defence operate under Hamas-run authorities, and the Cogat figures on deliveries are the Israeli military’s own claims that the sources do not independently verify.
items.op: Shelter for displaced families should not depend on whether a camp happens to sit below an unstable mound. The shift from five reported deaths to four shows why early figures from every side need checking against clear records. Disputes over what aid may enter should be settled openly, with published rules, not left to be argued through statements after each tragedy.
